description: We are Team TechoSpace, a passionate group focused on solving real-world challenges for space exploration. For this year’s NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are building intuitive health-monitoring software to track astronaut vital signs, physiological load, and well-being during long-duration missions. We’re looking for team members interested in UI/UX, software development, space medicine, or data analysis to help bring this project to life. Join us!
summary: Orbital Crew Health is an interactive web prototype exploring how astronaut health information could be organized during long-duration missions, when communication with Earth may be delayed. Users can select one of six sample telemetry scenarios or upload a compatible CSV, then replay the data with timeline and speed controls. The dashboard displays example heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiration, temperature, cabin CO₂, and radiation readings alongside an ECG visualization and scenario alerts. A mission-delay simulator demonstrates changing communication delays, while crew, body-map, and AURA assistant views let users explore other parts of the interface.This project is important because crews need clear access to health information when ground support is delayed. A local dashboard offers a starting point for exploring onboard decision-support tools. The current prototype uses local sample data; it does not connect to live sensors or NASA telemetry, and it does not provide clinical diagnosis or treatment. Future work includes validating the data and workflows with experts.
details:
Orbital Health is a web based prototype that explores how a crew health dashboard could support astronauts during missions where medical support from Earth may be delayed. Space crews work in unusual conditions, including microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, and disrupted sleep cycles. This project brings health signals and mission context into one interface, making it easier to explore how those factors might be monitored during a mission.

The application includes an overview page, a health dashboard, a crew section, an interactive body map, mission insights, alerts, and AURA, a conversational medical decision support demo. The dashboard presents heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), breathing rate, core temperature, cabin CO₂, and radiation measurements. It can play one of the bundled CSV scenarios or load a user selected CSV file. Users can pause and restart playback, change its speed, move through the timeline, inspect individual data rows, and view alerts when a scenario contains a flagged event.

The bundled scenarios demonstrate different situations, including a nominal baseline, exercise, a simulated oxygen related event, a solar radiation event, microgravity related fluid shifts, and an arrhythmia scenario. They give users a way to explore how changing values and events might appear on a dashboard. AURA can answer questions about topics such as SANS, cardiovascular adaptation, hypoxia, radiation, sleep, and exercise countermeasures. It can use Gemini 2.5 Flash through a server endpoint when a Gemini API key is configured. If that service is unavailable or not configured, the app falls back to built in rule based responses.

The body map connects selected areas of the body with spaceflight health topics and example measurements. The mission selector lets users explore different environments, including Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, and Europa, and illustrates how communication delay and mission conditions could affect onboard support. The interface also uses NASA imagery to give the project a clear space mission setting.

Orbital Health is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The dashboard uses the browser Canvas API to draw an ECG style trace, browser file handling to read CSV uploads, and a service worker and web app manifest to support installation as a Progressive Web App. An Electron setup provides an option to package the experience as a desktop application. The Gemini connection is handled through a server endpoint, keeping the API key on the server rather than in the browser code.

The project’s creative idea is to bring telemetry playback, visual health information, alerts, mission conditions, and a conversational assistant together in one experience. It is intended to help people explore how an onboard health support interface might work when communication is limited, and to make spaceflight health concepts easier to understand through interactive scenarios.

The current version is a demonstration prototype. The bundled telemetry scenarios are not live feeds from astronauts, the ECG trace is generated by the application rather than taken from a diagnostic device, and some body map values are illustrative. AURA is not a clinically validated medical system and should not be used to diagnose or treat a real person.

In designing the prototype, we considered delayed communication with Earth, the need to view several health signals together, offline access to core app resources, and the importance of making clear that simulated readings and AI generated guidance are not a substitute for clinical care.
